data.title: Woven Health Collective Earns Two Rx Club Awards for BridgeBio Immersive Education Program
data.description:
NEW YORK —

Woven Health Collective has earned two honors in the 2026 Rx Club Awards for “From Clues to Clarity: Recognizing ATTR-CM,” an immersive educational program created for BridgeBio. The program received recognition in the Augmented Reality and Educational Animation categories.

The virtual reality experience places health care professionals in the perspective of a patient living with undiagnosed transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, or ATTR-CM. Combining realistic animation with visual, audio, and haptic cues, the program was designed to reveal connections among symptoms that might otherwise be considered separately. 

“In health care, innovation is about more than demonstrating what a technology can do. It's about creatively deploying technology to serve an authentic need,” said Bart Zoni, Chief Digital, AI and Technology Officer of Woven Health Collective. “For this project, augmented reality created a unique learning moment for health care professionals while accommodating the requirements of scientific accuracy, the user experience, and medical, legal, and regulatory review from the start.”

Woven developed the experience in four months, combining character development, motion capture and symptom-based sensory effects. Its use extended from internal education for BridgeBio’s field force to HCP engagement at major medical conferences, illustrating how an immersive concept can be developed for practical use across different health care settings. 

“Our clients need partners who can co-create new ideas and understand what it takes to bring them to life within a life sciences company,” said Courtney Kaprelian, President of Woven Health Collective. “That requires creative ambition, respect for the science and an understanding of regulatory and compliance expectations. These honors recognize work that brings those priorities together rather than treating them as competing demands.”

The two Rx Club honors follow Woven’s November 9 announcement of a 2026 Healthcare Marketing Impact Award for the same program. Together, the recognitions highlight Woven’s focus on using technology to address specific challenges in HCP communication.

Learn more about Woven’s creative and AI capabilities at: https://www.wovenhc.com.

data.title: CXT Software, Dispatch Science Combine to Create Largest Unified Agentic Last-Mile TMS
data.description:
PHOENIX —

CXT Software announced today the acquisition of Dispatch Science, a cloud-native transportation management system (TMS) provider. The combined company unites the largest network of couriers in the last-mile market, and the deep workflow expertise of CXT and e-Courier with Dispatch Science’s modern cloud-native technology to accelerate the path to one unified, AI-driven and agentic TMS platform.
 

An Investment in Accelerating the Vision 

The acquisition is Ionic Partners’ next investment in the vision it set out in 2025, when it brought CXT and e-Courier together: an AI-driven, predictive and agentic TMS built on the latest technology and real-time data. The investment brings the strengths of all three companies together: more than 50 years of courier and compliance expertise, the deep workflows customers rely on, and modern, cloud-native technology. The result is one company moving toward one brand and one unified experience and code base that combines the best of each, where every new capability is built once, for every customer, and reaches the market faster.

— CXT Brings the Network: The largest network of couriers in the last-mile market, across North America, and 25 years of know-how running real operations. 

— e-Courier Brings the Workflow Depth: Workflow and compliance expertise, especially in healthcare, and extensive integrations built over 25 years. 

— Dispatch Science Brings the Modern Architecture: Cloud-native architecture built for AI and automation from day one, continuous real-time route optimization and live predictive ETAs, and an agile, founder-led team that ships quickly. 

 

From Predictive to Agentic 

Today’s TMS largely records what has already happened. The next generation predicts disruption and recommends the next best action. The destination is an agentic TMS that closes the loop and takes corrective action on its own: rerouting around a sudden road closure to protect a temperature-sensitive therapy, a time-critical specimen or an organ headed into surgery. It also rebalances thousands of everyday parcel stops across a fleet in real time, keeping cost per delivery down and on-time rates up, and it extends to deliveries by robots and drones as those models mature. 

“In 2025, we promised our customers an AI-driven, predictive and agentic TMS. That promise hasn’t changed. Today, we’re accelerating it,” said Lauren King, president of CXT Software. “Our customers move what matters most, from vaccines and organs to the millions of everyday parcels that keep businesses and households running. Every minute and every cent counts. Bringing the largest courier network, decades of compliance expertise and modern technology together in one unified platform gets us to that future faster, without disrupting what they rely on today.” 

“This is the biggest accelerator of our vision we could have imagined,” said Arthur Axelrad, co-founder of Dispatch Science. “Together, we start from a place it would have taken us three to five years to reach alone, with a much larger team behind every customer.” 

“We built Dispatch Science to be ready for whatever comes next,” said Alex Proteau, co-founder of Dispatch Science. “Paired with the workflow depth of CXT and e-Courier, that architecture lets us move from predictive to agentic faster than any of us could alone.” 

 

What’s Next for Customers 

Customers on CXT, e-Courier and Dispatch Science will see no immediate changes to their service, support or points of contact, and their teams stay focused on continuity. In February 2027, the combined company will introduce its unified brand and share its unified platform plan, including a first look at what agentic logistics will mean for their operations. Customers will hear about next steps directly, well ahead of any change and can contact their account team for updates.

data.title: Drugs from China are reshaping biotech. Track the licensing deals here.
data.description:
The makeup of the world’s pharmaceutical pipeline is changing. China’s fast-growing biotechnology industry is a big reason why. 

Over the past decade, China’s government has sought to upgrade the country’s drugmaking capabilities. Its efforts birthed a burgeoning ecosystem of homegrown companies and science parks that mirror — and even rival —  U.S. hubs in Boston and San Francisco. Lower costs and regulatory flexibility have helped China’s biotech startups move faster than their U.S. counterparts, producing a sprawling inventory of drug prospects. While many are designed to be superior versions of medicines either on the market or in development elsewhere, more and more are innovative, challenging the U.S.’s long-held biotech advantage. 

Large pharma companies and venture capital investors have taken note. Many are licensing experimental drugs from China, either to add to their drug portfolios or build new biotechs around. The shift has been rapid, with dealmaking spiking in recent years. According to analysts, licensing agreements hit a record pace in 2025. Fully one-third of the industry’s licensing spending in 2025 involved drugs sourced from China, per the investment bank Jefferies. That trajectory has accelerated in 2026.

These deals reveal important insights about the types of medicines drugmakers and investors want in their portfolios. With this database, we’re tracking deals from 2025 onward in which China-based drugmakers licensed to U.S. and European companies rights to human therapeutics. We show the companies involved, the financial terms of their alliances and details about the medicines and drug targets. 

If we’ve missed a deal, or there’s any additional information you’d like to see, please reach out and let us know.

Jump to database

Jump to methodology

Complex antibodies and small molecules are a popular target

Licensing agreements announced in 2025 and 2026

Cancer, immune disease drugs are drawing the most interest

Licensing agreements announced in 2025 and 2026

Deals typically involve early-stage drug candidates

Licensing agreements announced in 2025 and 2026

Licensing deals are getting bigger in size and scope

Licensing deals involving China-developed drugs

Database includes deals announced in 2025 and 2026 that involve a China-based biotechnology firm licensing a drug candidate or candidates to biopharmaceutical companies located in the U.S. or Europe.

Methodology

For this database, BioPharma Dive compiled deals announced in 2025 and 2026 through which China-based drugmakers licensed out innovative human medicines to biotech or pharmaceutical companies in the U.S. or Europe. 

We screened for these deals in company press releases, analyst reports and on social media sites like LinkedIn. We eliminated those that didn’t meet our criteria, including alliances that don’t mention any specific drug candidates or partnerships between two China-based companies. We also excluded deals involving generic drugs or biosimilars.

We generally used a deal’s most advanced program to determine the therapeutic area of focus, treatment type and stage of development at the time of a deal’s announcement. We categorized phase of development by the latest stage underway at the time of a deal.

Therapeutic areas cover a large number of diseases and, in some cases, overlap. In most cases, when companies identified more than one therapeutic area with equal priority, we classified them as working on “multiple” therapeutic areas. Companies that identified multiple areas, but prioritized one over others were classified under that priority area.

Ned Pagliarulo contributed reporting.

data.title: Completing the circle: the next evolution in sustainable pharmaceutical blister packaging
data.description:
Sustainability has become a driving force behind many of the strategic decisions being made by pharmaceutical manufacturers. From material selection and packaging design to manufacturing efficiency and end-of-life considerations, the industry is increasingly looking for ways to reduce its environmental footprint without compromising product protection, regulatory compliance and patient safety.

One area where significant progress has been made is in pharmaceutical blister packaging. Traditionally, blister packages have relied on combinations of dissimilar materials, making recycling difficult. Thus, sustainability efforts have focused primarily on existing blister and tray materials through downgauging and/or incorporating recycled content.

Despite these advancements, one component has largely remained unchanged: the lidding material. Traditional aluminum foil lidding continues to be widely used, creating a material mismatch when paired with polymer-based blister trays. While the bottom web may be designed for recycling, the complete package remains a combination of different material types, limiting its potential for recovery.

Recent innovations in polymer engineering are beginning to address this gap. Advances in peelable sealant technology have made it possible to develop lidding materials compatible with the same polymer families used in today's most common blister packaging materials. By bringing the forming web and lidding into alignment, pharmaceutical manufacturers now have an opportunity to create complete mono-material blister systems designed with recycling in mind.

Expanding options with mono-material packaging

Polyester (PET) is becoming an established material in pharmaceutical blister packaging for certain applications. PET is valued for its clarity, dimensional stability and thermal performance. With the development of compatible polyester lidding materials, manufacturers can now move toward all-PET blister packaging systems without relying on traditional foil-based constructions.

These lidding structures combine a PET film with an engineered peelable polyester sealant layer. Designed to provide controlled peel seals to APET blister materials, they offer a fully functional mono-polymer whole package solution can be achieved.

Beyond material compatibility, polyester lidding offers advantages in demanding processing environments. Its inherent thermal stability supports high-temperature applications, while certain constructions are also suitable for gamma sterilization. Transparent appearance, and a peelable seal for both child resistance and improved senior friendliness, provide additional flexibility for packaging applications.

The combination of compatible PET forming webs and lidding materials creates an opportunity for a complete all-polyester package. Certain systems have also achieved third-party recyclability certification, demonstrating the potential of mono-material design to support improved recovery within established recycling frameworks.

Polypropylene (PP) is another widely used material in pharmaceutical blister packaging, offering manufacturers an alternative polymer platform for developing more sustainable package systems. As PP forming webs become increasingly available, compatible lidding materials are an important next step.

Newer all-polypropylene lidding constructions combine a high-barrier PP film with a peelable polypropylene sealant. Designed to seal to PP blister materials, these structures provide an opportunity to create a complete mono-material package while maintaining important functional requirements.

Barrier performance is particularly important in certain pharmaceutical applications, where packaging must help protect products from environmental exposure throughout their intended shelf life. Engineered PP lidding materials can provide outstanding moisture barrier properties, along with good oxygen and aroma barrier characteristics. Similar peelable seal performance and transparent appearance further expand their potential applications.

For manufacturers looking to transition toward more sustainable packaging, these constructions offer a recycle-ready approach designed for the polypropylene collection stream. Importantly, compatible PP lidding offers flexibility to continue utilizing existing PP bottom-web materials rather than requiring a complete redesign of established blister packaging platforms.

Moving toward complete packaging solutions

The evolution of pharmaceutical blister packaging illustrates an important shift in how sustainability goals are being approached. Rather than focusing on individual packaging components, manufacturers are increasingly considering the complete package system and how material choices influence its potential end-of-life recovery.

Advancements in both PET and PP lidding demonstrate that meaningful improvements do not necessarily require manufacturers to abandon established forming materials or overhaul their existing packaging designs. By introducing compatible lidding technologies, it is now possible to bring previously disconnected packaging components together into more cohesive, mono-material systems.

While recycling infrastructure and collection capabilities remain important considerations, continued innovation in material science is helping the pharmaceutical industry move closer to its sustainability goals without losing sight of the fundamental purpose of packaging: protecting the product and ultimately the patient.

Learn more

To learn more about PAXXUS’ commercially available all-PET StreamOne® Px and all-PP StreamFive® Px pharmaceutical lidding solutions, including PAXXUS material technologies, technical specifications and application capabilities, visit the PAXXUS website.

data.title: Elusa Health Launches Foresight Analytics Platform to Transform Patient Access Hub Data
data.description:
MAITLAND, Fla. —

ORLANDO, F.L., NOVEMBER 16, 2026 - Elusa Health, a leading hub services company supporting specialty pharmaceutical and biopharma manufacturers, today announced the launch of Foresight, an analytics platform that transforms hub program data into actionable intelligence. Built directly into the Elusa Health patient hub services ecosystem, Foresight visually renders program performance data to help manufacturers visualize where payers, prescribers, and processes slow patients down, and gives their teams the visibility to remove bottlenecks and make smarter, data-informed decisions. 

Closing the visibility gap in patient access

Hub programs generate thousands of data points on every patient journey, from benefits verification and prior authorization to therapy start. For most manufacturers, that data has been scattered across systems and reports, leaving brand and access teams to assemble the full picture themselves.

"Our clients have been telling us the same thing for a long time," said Era Prakash, SVP of Solutions Development at Elusa Health. "This level of detail either wasn't accessible to them, or getting it meant pulling from multiple sources and piecing it together. By the time the picture came together, the moment to make decisions and act had often passed. Foresight puts that detail in one place, inside the portal they can access directly, so teams spend their time acting on insights instead of assembling them."

Foresight updates daily and uses configurable templates that adjust to each program's KPIs, so dashboards reflect the most meaningful data points for that brand.

One platform, two offerings

Foresight is available as two commercial offerings on a single platform, so programs can start with essential reporting and grow into advanced analytics without changing systems.

Foundation delivers the reporting essentials every program needs to see performance and trends:

  • Case volumes, approval rates, and PA/BV completions
  • Patient success funnel views showing case submissions through patient outcomes
  • Curated dashboards that surface the highest-value KPIs
  • Baseline analytics on trends and variances across select client KPIs

Intelligence is a growing suite of advanced analytics that turns data into decision-ready insights. It includes full access to Foundation, plus:

  • Prescriber and site-level activity and enrollment rates, root cause analysis on patient drop-off, payer performance and segmentation, and sentiment analysis from call monitoring that flags recurring friction before it grows.
  • Predictive capabilities that use machine learning to anticipate what's next, including PA required/not required forecasting, therapy approval turnaround time, and seasonal patient forecasting. 

Foresight has planned capabilities to be added over time, including AI-enabled recommendations, additional data sources, and cross-program intelligence. Elusa Health will continue to expand the Foresight KPI library and capabilities, with new functionality added to the platform as it becomes available.

"Meaningful data has never mattered more," said Bill Nolan, CEO of Elusa Health. "Manufacturers are being asked to do more with tighter budgets and leaner teams. Resource constraints don't mean patients need our help any less. They mean we have to get surgical about where we focus, and that starts with data. Foresight shows our partners exactly where patients are getting stuck and where support makes the biggest difference, so every dollar and every hour goes where it counts."

Foresight is available as a part of the Elusa Health suite of patient hub services. Learn more at elusahealth.com/foresight.

data.title: Biotech M&A is accelerating. Track the deals that are happening here.
data.description:
In the business of drug development, deals can be just as important as scientific breakthroughs. Many of today's most lucrative medicines, from the life-saving cancer treatment Keytruda to the anti-inflammatory agent Enbrel, might not have become so without mergers and acquisitions.

The end of the last decade brought record highs in pharmaceutical M&A as larger companies turned again and again to young biotechs for innovation. Often, these deals focused on cancer, rare diseases and immune system disorders — areas of drug research that were seeing major victories in clinical trials and huge profits for treatments that made it to market.

2021 and 2022 were much quieter for dealmaking, as new challenges and then rising interest rates weighed on negotiations. But there have been signs of a rebound. Pharma companies are keen to expand in areas like obesity, while stocking up on newer technologies like antibody-drug conjugates. Even neuroscience, which large drugmakers previously abandoned, is drawing investment again.

BioPharma Dive is tracking M&A activity below. The database, which shows drugmaker buyouts that have happened since 2018 and were valued at $50 million or more in upfront consideration, will be regularly updated.

Click on an acquiring company to pull up more information, and scroll to the bottom of the page to read how this information was collected and organized. If there's anything we've missed, or any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.

data.title: This week in charts: Brain drugs are back on venture capitalists’ minds
data.description:
This is the latest installment in a series where BioPharma Dive uses data visualization to recap what’s going on across the industry. Today, we’re looking at renewed interest in brain drugs and a muted investor response to the latest cell therapy research.

Despite its reputation as one of the most challenging and risky areas of drug research, neuroscience had, over the last several years, started to gain momentum among venture capitalists. Between 2023 and 2025, startups focused on the central nervous system took in $1.09 billion, $1.58 billion and $1.9 billion from 26 prolific venture firms, according to data compiled by BioPharma Dive.

While the 2026 total hasn’t been as large, at $664 million by mid-November, a recent funding tear signals that brain drugs can still draw investors’ attention. Just this week, London-based Oyster Therapeutics said it had raised $60 million from a Series A round that was led by 4BIO Capital and saw participation from eight other parties, including pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly. Oyster’s aim is to degrade a notorious protein with ties to Alzheimer’s disease.

Four other neuroscience biotechs — Setara Therapeutics, Delix Therapeutics, VectorY Therapeutics and Neurosterix — disclosed fundraising hauls since the end of October. Those rounds collectively brought in around $400 million.

A flurry of recent deals helped prop up what’s been a less active year for neuroscience VC

Five rounds in recent weeks added around $450 million to this year’s haul.

Elsewhere, public market investors had a mostly negative response to the latest data from some cell therapy developers who presented data this week at the American College of Rheumatology conference.

The annual meeting offered the latest look into how these cutting-edge therapies are faring against immune disorders like lupus and an uncommon condition known as systemic sclerosis. Philadelphia-based Cabaletta Bio, for instance, reported early, encouraging results from a trial testing its therapy “rese-cel” across three different diseases. The biotech’s share price has risen roughly 5% since the market’s close last week.

Conversely, shares of Nkarta, Allogene Therapeutics and Fate Therapeutics were all down more than 20% from Nov. 6 to Nov. 12. CRISPR Therapeutics also declined nearly 15%.

Investors largely balk at new research updates from cell therapy developers

Nkarta, Allogene and Fate were especially hard hit.

Perhaps the best stock performance over the past few days was PepGen, whose experimental treatment for a muscle-wasting illness impressed Wall Street analysts.

According to PepGen, a mid-stage study of people with “myotonic dystrophy type 1” found the company’s drug helped repair, on average, 46.5% of the “splicing errors” that are a genetic hallmark of the disease. PepGen described the outcome as the “highest level of splicing correction ever” in a study testing multiple doses of a drug for this condition. And its stock subsequently surged north of 90%.

PepGen shares rocketed more than 90% earlier this week

At least one analyst now sees the company’s drug as competitive with rival medicines from Novartis and Dyne Therapeutics.

Joseph Schwartz, an analyst at Leerink Partners, wrote in a note to clients that PepGen’s figure is higher than what researchers have seen with rival therapies from Novartis and Dyne Therapeutics. And while “cross-trial comparisons remain imperfect,” he added, “the magnitude and consistency” of the results “support clear best-in-class potential.”

data.title: Big-name investors pour $100M into DNA therapeutics developer Seawolf
data.description:
Seawolf Therapeutics, a San Diego company with a cache of well-known life sciences investors, emerged from stealth on Monday, equipped with $100 million to support its research into DNA-based therapies.

Seawolf’s founding investor, Versant Ventures, led its seed funding and participated in a Series A round alongside other prominent biotechnology backers like MPM BioImpact, Alexandria Venture Investments and others. The financing also drew interest from fellow drug companies, with Eli Lilly, CRISPR Therapeutics and the venture arm of Novartis all contributing.

As part of its debut, Seawolf disclosed a partnership with French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi. Though sparse on details, the research collaboration and exclusive license agreement will be “multi-target,” and focus on developing therapies for bleeding disorders and additional unnamed indications. Seawolf could take home as much as $1.2 billion across various milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on any resulting products.

“With a strong syndicate of investors and our collaboration with Sanofi, we are well-positioned to execute on our next stage of growth, which will include advancing our lead program for metabolic diseases and collaborating with Sanofi in its mission to develop therapies for patient unmet needs,” said Elizabeth Alcamo, Seawolf’s CEO, in a statement.

Seawolf is built around a technology that uses a protective casing of fat molecules — known as lipid nanoparticles, or LNPs for short — to deliver beneficial packages of genetic material into cells. Specifically, this “TRIDENT” platform takes DNA that’s been engineered to avoid triggering an immune system response and places it into a proprietary LNP.

That nanoparticle then, with help from an additional “auxiliary” component, shepherds the DNA into the nucleus, where it provides the instructions for making proteins that combat disease. Drugs made from this system share all the pros of RNA-based LNP therapies, according to Seawolf, but with the added benefit of longer-lasting expression.

The company claims that, in primate tests, medicines created with its technology were potent, durable and safe. And unlike technology platforms that use viruses to deliver DNA payloads, TRIDENT therapies can be redosed, offering “the ability to fine-tune or supplement dosing through repeated administration.”

“Nucleic acid-based therapies have advanced dramatically over the past decade,” said Tom Woiwode, a managing director at Versant and chair of Seawolf’s board, in a statement. The startup’s team is “now delivering on the promise of using DNA to drive robust and long-term expression of therapeutic proteins directly from the patient’s own cells.”

Seawolf said its system can be useful across a “broad range” of diseases, including both rare and prevalent ones, and that it worked as intended in both primate and mouse models of metabolic and rare diseases.

The company’s lead program goes after metabolic diseases — an area of venture capital investment that, as of late, has cooled a bit. So far this year, emerging drugmakers in this field have received about $740 million from 26 of the most prolific biotech venture firms, according to data compiled by BioPharma Dive. That’s down from the nearly $1.3 billion and $1.6 billion seen in 2025 and 2024, respectively.

data.title: Cibus Therapeutics and Greenstone Biosciences Announce First Participant Dosed in Phase 1 Trial of CBT-248 (GSB-D248), an Investigational Oral Anti-Inflammatory Therapy for Chronic Pancreatitis
data.description:
PALO ALTO, Calif. —

Cibus Therapeutics and Greenstone Biosciences today announced that the first participant has been dosed in a Phase 1 clinical trial of CBT-248 (GSB-D248), an investigational oral small-molecule therapy being developed for chronic pancreatitis and ulcerative colitis. The trial is being conducted in Australia.

CBT-248 was developed at Greenstone Biosciences and is exclusively licensed to Cibus Therapeutics, which is leading its clinical development. The compound is designed to modulate multiple inflammatory pathways, with preclinical studies demonstrating efficacy in models of chronic pancreatitis and ulcerative colitis.

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive fibro-inflammatory disease of the pancreas that causes severe, often intractable pain, irreversible tissue damage, and loss of digestive and endocrine function. It is estimated to affect approximately 3 million people worldwide and is associated with an increased risk of pancreatic cancer. No approved disease-modifying therapy exists; current care is limited to managing symptoms and complications.

Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by persistent inflammation and ulceration of the colon, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, urgency, and fatigue. Despite advances in treatment, many patients experience inadequate responses, loss of efficacy, or intolerance to existing therapies, highlighting the continued need for safer and more effective treatments that provide sustained disease control.

The Phase 1 study is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-ascending-dose study evaluating the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of CBT-248 in healthy adult volunteers. The study plans to enroll 32 participants across four dose cohorts at Nucleus Network in Melbourne, Australia, and includes an assessment of the effect of food on drug exposure. Additional details are available on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07905053) and ANZCTR (ACTRN12626001257358). 

Data from the trial are intended to inform dose selection and the design of subsequent clinical studies in patients with chronic pancreatitis and ulcerative colitis. Cibus expects topline safety, tolerability and PK data in Q2 2027.

"Taking GSB-D248 from discovery through IND-enabling studies meant answering one question at every step: will what we see in the lab hold up in people?" said Mukhtar Ahmed, PhD, Director of Project & Portfolio Strategy at Greenstone Biosciences, who led the compound's preclinical development. "Seeing the first participant dosed is the start of getting that answer. Our team is proud to have handed Cibus a program built to make that transition, and we will keep supporting it as it moves toward patients."

“Dosing the first participant marks an important milestone in advancing CBT-248 from preclinical research into clinical development,” said Honit Piplani, PhD, Director of Translational and Clinical Science at Cibus Therapeutics. “People living with chronic pancreatitis face persistent pain, difficulty eating and uncertainty about their future, and there is no approved therapy that targets the underlying disease. This first study will establish the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics we need to design studies in patients, and we are grateful to our partners at Greenstone Biosciences for helping us reach this point.”

"This milestone reflects the discovery and translational work our team put into CBT-248 (GSB-D248)," said Joseph Wu, MD, PhD, Co-founder of Greenstone Biosciences and a Professor of Medicine & Radiology at Stanford University. "We built the preclinical package on human-relevant models to give the program the strongest possible footing for the clinic. We delivered on the plan we set with Cibus, and we look forward to supporting the program as it advances toward patients."

data.title: BIO unveils plan for US to remain biotech’s ‘global leader’
data.description:
Two months after China unveiled a five-year plan to accelerate the ascent of its fast-rising biotechnology sector, a prominent lobbying group is pitching a policy proposal designed to help the U.S. maintain an edge in the field.

The “action plan” by the Biotechnology Innovation Organization unveiled Tuesday lays out seven priorities Congress and the Trump administration should act on to “ensure” the U.S. remains the sector’s “global leader.” Called “BioAdvance: Securing America’s Biotech Century,” it involves ways to speed up drug development, improve the nation's clinical trial infrastructure, attract investment and better support biomedical research.

BIO also calls on the U.S. to establish a “White House Office of Biotechnology” to help coordinate these plans and keep them on track. 

“This moment demands the ambition and determination that catalyzed the biotechnology revolution and made America the definitive global leader,” said BIO President and CEO John Crowley in a statement.

BIO’s proposal comes amid an escalating debate among biotech executives, investors and lawmakers as to how to respond to China’s emergence as a drugmaking force. The U.S. has long been the world’s standard-bearer in developing new medicines. Yet China has made biotech progress a strategic priority and invested heavily in the sector over the last decade or so.

That effort is now “paying off,” according to BIO. China now starts more than a quarter of the world’s clinical trials and initiates early-stage studies more quickly and cheaply. Dealmaking involving China-originated medicines has exploded of late, too. More than 100 licensing deals have been struck between Western pharmaceutical firms or biotechs and Chinese drugmakers, according to BioPharma Dive data.

China aims to make further inroads in the future. In a five-year plan released in September, the Chinese government indicated its goal is to develop at least a quarter of the world’s “first-in-class drugs” by 2030. 

So far, the U.S. has waffled between trying to slow down China’s progress or boost its own sector. The Treasury Department, for instance, has floated a proposal to add biotech to the “COINS” Act, which could limit some deals and draw greater scrutiny to U.S. biotech investments in China. That approach has yielded criticism from BIO, whose leader Crowley warned in October that the U.S. “cannot restrict our way to success.”

“We need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors, and that may unintentionally risk weakening U.S. biotech competitiveness,” Crowley said in a statement at the time.

Prominent biotech investment firms such as RA Capital Management have voiced similar criticisms, claiming putting biotech into the COINS Act “does nothing to shore up domestic manufacturing or restrict the ability of Chinese companies to control distribution of medicines.”

Meanwhile, U.S. regulators have unveiled programs to speed up clinical testing and make the U.S. a more attractive destination for starting first-in-human studies. 

Now, BIO is trying to push the federal government to go further. Its proposal includes several ways to improve drugmaking efficiency in the U.S. while addressing structural weaknesses that slow down clinical research. Investors and CEOs interviewed by BioPharma Dive said the plan, which focuses more on shoring up America’s capabilities rather than striking back at China, is achievable and a welcome move.

“I think it’s a great list,” said Lindy Morris Fishburne, a managing partner at Breakout Ventures, which invests in early-stage life sciences startups. “But the world moves on incentives and people, and if those things are not aligned, then policy doesn’t matter.”

In its report, BIO pushed legislators and the Food and Drug Administration to adopt more flexible requirements for starting first-in-human trials, prioritize modernized alternatives to animal testing and centralize many of the processes required before testing can begin. 

“Biotechnology companies must be able to efficiently test the safety and dosage of their innovations — and iterate quickly based on those results — to attract investment for early-stage research,” the organization wrote in its proposal. 

The U.S.’ clinical trial network is currently “siloed and unevenly distributed,” creating capacity constraints for specialized Phase 1 studies and slowing down early research. As a result, many U.S.-based companies are conducting an increasing share of their early-stage drug development in countries such as China and Australia, “where the process is often faster, more predictable, and less expensive,” BIO said.

Quralis, a Cambridge, Massachusetts-based brain drug developer, launched several of its proof-of-concept trials outside of the U.S. “because the regulatory framework was not conducive” to doing so at home, said Kasper Roet, the company’s CEO.

The proposal suggests that U.S. regulators engage earlier with drug developers and clearly lay out expectations during meetings. BIO also wants policymakers to centralize approval processes across local clinical trial sites, expand the network of testing locations and create “user-friendly” tools to help doctors and patients find trials.

But those efforts — and any future plans to speed up human testing — hinge on having a fully staffed agency and leadership motivated to make those changes, according to Fishburne.

“You're going to have all this incredible technology advancing pipelines, lowering risk and answering questions earlier, and then you're going to hit this old-time bureaucratic wall,” she said.

BIO previously told the FDA in a public comment that its pilot program to accelerate early testing contains only “incremental improvements” to application reviews that are “unlikely to materially shift the timelines” for those trials or reverse the ongoing trend. Fishburne said the FDA’s efforts are welcome, but “feel more like disconnected green shoots rather than [an] overarching strategy.”

The proposal also calls on the Trump administration to put more money toward basic research through the National Institutes of Health. Last year, biotech investors and academics warned of dire long-term consequences for the life sciences if the government significantly cut NIH grant funding. Though a federal court ultimately barred a plan to cap NIH funding, many institutions are still affected by delays in grant renewals and sharp drops in dollars headed toward certain types of research, one NPR report found.

“Providing ample and predictable federal research funding” and establishing “reliable pathways” to attract talent to American universities are additional cornerstones of BIO’s proposal.

Strengthening the NIH and streamlining early clinical research are particularly important parts of BIO’s request, said Chris Bardon, a managing partner at the venture firm MPM BioImpact.

“NIH research has always been the name of the game,” Bardon said. “To really undermine that is, at the end of the day, what's going to harm the long-term competitiveness of our basic science as well as of our biotechnology industry.”

BIO pointed to other legislative initiatives to spur venture capital funding and protect intellectual property rights. Policymakers “should also reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens and adopt tax and economic incentives that encourage investment in innovative startups,” the organization wrote.

A new White House Office of Biotechnology could help carry these initiatives out and ensure the government adopts a “unified national strategy.” That office could also help identify "key policy priorities to promote U.S. biotech competitiveness" and coordinate plans with "trusted allies.” 

Bardon said the BioAdvance plan could turn into a “bipartisan effort” to shore up an industry that has been “taken for granted.”

“The rise of China has woken up the United States to realize we were very comfortable being in the leading position, but now that is being challenged,” said Roet, Quralis’ CEO.
